holding_summary: After a Canara Bank employee died intestate, his widow and his mother both claimed posthumous terminal benefits of about Rs. 62.90 lakh, with the mother relying on her status as the nominee recorded in the bank's records. Justice Biraja Prasanna Satapathy held that nomination in a bank account or insurance policy does not amount to ownership — a nominee merely holds the proceeds as a trustee for the legal heirs — and that under Hindu succession law the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolves first upon his Class I heirs, including his widow, ahead of any nominee's claim.
why_it_matters: A bank, insurer or company nominee recorded on an account or policy is not thereby made the legal owner of the proceeds — the deceased's actual legal heirs under succession law retain the superior claim, so families should not assume a nomination alone settles who is entitled to a deceased relative's funds.

case_name: Sri Venkataiah v. State of Karnataka & Ors.
holding_summary: An 84-year-old illiterate senior citizen sought annulment of a gift deed executed in favour of his daughters, contending it was drafted at his daughters' instance with him merely affixing a thumb impression without understanding its contents, and that the assurance to maintain him — though the very basis of the transfer — had been deliberately omitted from the document. The Karnataka High Court held that a legal representative of the original donee cannot independently resist annulment of a gift deed under Section 23 of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 by raising derivative defences that were unavailable to the donee, once the statutory conditions for revocation are otherwise met.
why_it_matters: A senior citizen seeking to reclaim property transferred in exchange for an implied or express promise of maintenance can have that gift deed annulled even where the promise was never written into the document, and the donee's own legal heirs cannot resist that annulment by raising defences the original donee themselves could not have raised.

case_name: Ashok Shankar v. Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax
court: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Delhi Bench
holding_summary: The taxpayer had failed to disclose a foreign bank account and his shareholding in a UAE company in his income tax return. The Delhi Bench of the ITAT upheld the income tax demand and penalty levied under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, holding that a foreign bank account cannot be left undisclosed merely because it has few transactions, and that non-disclosure of a foreign asset — together with a failure to explain its source — attracts action under the Act even where some related income was otherwise reported.
why_it_matters: NRIs and returning residents with foreign bank accounts or overseas shareholdings should treat full Schedule FA disclosure in their Indian income tax return as non-negotiable — a dormant account with minimal activity, or a shareholding whose related income was reported elsewhere, does not excuse leaving the underlying asset itself undisclosed.

case_name: Gur Kaur (Minor) & Ors. v. Union of India & Anr.
holding_summary: Adoptive parents who had completed a registered adoption of a minor child under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, including verification by the District Magistrate, sought CARA's No Objection Certificate to relocate the child to Canada, but CARA issued only a support letter rather than the NOC needed for the destination country's immigration process. Justice Sachin Datta held that CARA is statutorily obligated under the Adoption Regulations to facilitate compliance with the Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption for such relocations, and cannot leave adoptive parents without effective recourse merely because the underlying adoption was completed under HAMA rather than the Juvenile Justice Act.
why_it_matters: Families who have adopted a child under Hindu personal law and later need to relocate abroad now have High Court authority that CARA cannot fob them off with an informal support letter — it must actively process Hague Convention documentation needed for the destination country to recognise the adoption and grant the child entry.

case_name: In re: Adoption of a Minor by an NRI Relative (US-based aunt) v. Union of India (CARA)
holding_summary: A 13-year-old girl, adopted under a registered adoption deed by her maternal aunt and uncle (resident in the United States) under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 following her mother's death in July 2024, challenged a CARA office memorandum of 9 February 2026 that blocked processing of the inter-country relative adoption. At a hearing on 22 June 2026, a Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Joymalya Bagchi questioned CARA's opposition to adoption by close family members and expressed dissatisfaction with the administrative hurdles facing relatives seeking to care for the child, listing the matter for further hearing; the case remains pending and no final order has issued as of the date of this note.
why_it_matters: NRI relatives seeking to formalise or relocate a child already adopted by them under personal law should watch this case closely — the Supreme Court's early remarks suggest it may curb CARA's practice of treating a relative adoption already completed under HAMA as ineligible for inter-country adoption clearance, though the point is not yet finally decided.
